Redwood AE + SE walked through runbook, failover options across Hosted/Dedicated/Private, KMS encryption, audit logs and SSO/RBAC mappings. Agreed to share runbook and schedule a tabletop exercise.
transcript:
Header: 2026-05-14 15:00 UTC | Duration: 46m | Attendees: Maya, Liam, Sofia (Redwood) / Aisha, Tom, Priya, Evan (Galactic Bank)

[00:00] Maya (Redwood): Hi everyone, thanks for joining, appreciate you making time. we're gonna run through our incident response and BCDR playbook and then take questions.
[00:18] Aisha (Galactic Bank): Thanks Maya, quick context — Galactic is in final stages of vendor review, CISOs asking for concrete RTOs and how the escalation flow works. We'll also need KMS separation details and audit log retention.
[00:32] Maya: Yep understood. Liam will go deeper on the technical failover options. high level first: Redwood provides Hosted API with our multi-az control plane, Dedicated pools for reserved capacity, and Private deploy for VPC/on-prem. Our BCDR differentiates by deployment mode.
[00:50] Liam (Redwood SE): Hey all — quick note on nomenclature, RTO we generally target 5–15 minutes for control plane failover in hosted for most customers, but for Dedicated or Private it depends on customer's infra and chosen replication. RPO for stateless requests is near zero for live KV cache in our dedicated pool if enabled, but for long-term state we recommend async replication — typical RPO target we propose is 1 hour unless you need lower.
[01:15] Tom (Galactic): When you say 'control plane failover', can you clarify what that includes — DNS, model routing, and KV caches?
[01:23] Liam: Good question. Control plane failover covers orchestration, routing decisions, model variant fallback. DNS is handled via our global endpoints with weighted routing; we do a health-check and shift traffic. KV cache is more of a node-level concern — we have optional cross-zone KV replication but that's extra configuration. FYI sometimes docs show 'KV cash' in older drafts — ignore that typo.
[01:48] Priya (Galactic): On the KMS side, is customer-managed keys supported across Hosted and Dedicated? We need evidence of key separation and no plaintext access in logs.
[01:58] Maya: Yes, customer-managed keys supported for Hosted via our KMS integration (AWS KMS, GCP KMS) and Dedicated/Private can use HSM/KMS in your VPC. Logs do not contain plaintext model inputs — we redact PII by default in audit logs but customers can opt to retain full payloads for debugging with additional controls.
[02:18] Evan (Galactic): What about SLA — we need guaranteed uptime and credits. Typical financial procurement wants 99.95% or higher.
[02:25] Maya: Our standard Dedicated SLA is 99.95% with defined credits. Hosted has a different profile but we can discuss committed throughput and response targets under contract. For Private deployments uptime depends on your infra; Redwood's control plane optional HA can be part of the contract.
[02:40] Aisha: Can you walk me through an actual incident timeline and escalation path — for example a regional GPU cloud outage?
[02:49] Liam: Sure — I'll outline the runbook steps. Step 1: detection — automated alerts from Prometheus/Datadog and our health-checks. Step 2: classification — S1 if production-wide impact, S2 degraded performance. Step 3: immediate mitigation — traffic reroute to healthy region or fallback model variant. Step 4: incident commander assigned within 5 minutes for S1, with Redwood on-call pager escalation to SE and AE.
[03:18] Tom: Who is the incident commander on Redwood side?
[03:22] Sofia (Redwood CSM): We assign an on-call incident commander from our SRE roster for escalations; for dedicated customers we can also nominate a named technical account owner per the contract.
[03:31] Aisha: And then after mitigation, what's the postmortem cadence?
[03:35] Liam: Postmortems are done within 72 hours for S1, we share timeline, root cause analysis, remediation steps. For regulated customers we can provide a redacted RCA and detailed logs under NDA.
[03:49] Priya: Regarding audit logs, how long are they retained, and can we push them to our SIEM?
[03:55] Maya: Default retention is 90 days in the console, longer retention is an add-on. We provide integrations to stream audit logs to customer SIEMs via S3/GCS destinations or syslog endpoints.
[04:10] Evan: Do audit logs ever include model outputs? We must avoid exfiltration of regulated data.
[04:15] Liam: We aim to avoid model output in logs. By default audit logs include request metadata, user id, route, and token usage. If a customer requires full request/response logging for debugging, that's opt-in and comes with controls — encryption at rest and restricted access, and we recommend using customer-managed KMS.
[04:34] [15s pause — note: brief network blip]
[04:50] Speaker 2 (unknown / transcription artefact): ah yeah, so um —
[04:55] Maya: Sorry about the blip. Back to escalation: our pager escalation goes to L2 SRE, then L3 engineering triage, and then product leadership if it meets the severity threshold. We can provide a matrix that maps severity to SLA credit percentages.
[05:12] Aisha: We need RTO/RPO examples for different modes — can you provide a matrix?
[05:18] Liam: Yes. Quick example off the cuff: Hosted control plane failover RTO ~10–15m, RPO near zero for ephemeral requests if cache replication on; Dedicated with active-active cross-zone can be sub-5m RTO with similar RPO if KV replication enabled; Private/on-prem RTO is variable and depends on your DR topology — we typically see 30m–2h without automation. We'll include a formal table in the doc.
[05:45] Tom: Any tests or exercises you run to validate RTO/RPO?
[05:50] Sofia: We recommend quarterly DR tabletop and annual failover drills. Redwood can run assisted failovers in a staging window — we do canary failovers and measure observed RTO. We'll propose dates in the follow-up.
[06:07] Priya: Escalation contacts — can we get a named escalation list and SLAs for response time? For example, 15m initial response for S1?
[06:15] Maya: Yes our typical contractual response SLA for S1 is 15 minutes acknowledgement and 1 hour remediation steps; final resolution depends on root cause. We'll put specifics in the SOW.
[06:26] Evan: For Dedicated, how do you handle data residency during failover? If we failover to another region, are we exposing data to different legal jurisdictions?
[06:35] Liam: Important point. For customers with data residency requirements, we support regional pinned deployments — failover stays within allowed regions. Cross-region failover is optional and documented; we can restrict cross-region transfer in policy.
[06:49] Aisha: On compliance attestation, we need evidence of SOC 2 and ISO controls mapped to your runbook steps.
[06:57] Maya: We have a SOC 2 Type II report and ISO 27001 cert — we'll share the latest reports under NDA and include a control mapping doc that ties their cert sections to our operational checks in the runbook.
[07:10] Tom: How do we do SSO/SCIM provisioning for on-call rotations and RBAC? We need least-privilege access for our compliance team.
[07:18] Liam: We support SAML SSO and SCIM provisioning for groups. RBAC has roles like Admin, Engineer, ReadOnly, and SupportAccess. For critical incidents you can grant temporary elevated roles through ephemeral sessions; SCIM can sync group membership from your identity provider.
[07:34] Priya: Is there an audit trail for who executed a failover or changed ACLs?
[07:38] Maya: Yes, all admin actions are logged with user id and timestamp. We can provide immutable audit exports to your SIEM.
[07:46] [Timestamp jump to 22:00 mark in call for longer discussion]
[22:01] Liam: I want to call out one architecture pattern — active-passive dedicated with warm standby in a separate AZ: warm nodes maintain replicated KV and model artifacts; when primary fails we promote standby and route traffic. This reduces cold-start model load but requires slightly higher cost.
[22:23] Tom: Cost tradeoffs are fine as long as we meet RTO targets. Need to quantify.
[22:28] Maya: We'll include cost delta estimates for warm standby vs cold rebuild in the follow-up spreadsheet.
[22:34] Aisha: In a regulatory audit, how do we show chain of custody for a logged request?
[22:39] Liam: We can provide a stitched timeline — request id, timestamped events, operator actions, and storage location. For sensitive requests we recommend redaction and using customer-managed KMS so only you can decrypt bodies.
[23:00] Priya: What about tabletop exercises — what do they look like?
[23:05] Sofia: Typically 2 hours: scenario walkthrough, roles assigned, simulated outage, decision points, and then a 45–60m hotwash to capture improvements. We'd include our runbook and post-exercise action list.
[23:20] Evan: On the escalation matrix — do we have on-call rotations that overlap with our EMEA hours? We need 24/7 coverage.
[23:28] Maya: Redwood SREs cover 24/7; we can also set up a joint on-call for your SREs depending on the contract.
[23:36] [Minor crosstalk]
[23:40] Aisha: Walk me through an example escalation to legal — if there's potential data exposure, how quickly do you notify?
[23:48] Liam: If PII or regulated data is suspected to be exposed, we escalate to legal and C-suite per the incident classification, typically within 1–2 hours for S1. Notification timelines are set in the contract and aligned to breach notification laws.
[24:05] Maya: We'll include a redlined notification timeline based on your jurisdiction — please send the primary legal contact in the action items.
[24:15] Tom: Are there automatic safeguards to throttle or pause requests if anomalous behavior is detected?
[24:21] Liam: Yes, we have rate-limiters and anomaly detectors; we can set thresholds per customer and route suspected traffic for human review, and optionally pause ingestion while investigating.
[24:36] Aisha: On the backup front, what's your backup cadence for model artifacts and configuration?
[24:42] Maya: Model artifacts are stored in immutable object storage with versioning. We snapshot configs daily and replicate to a second region. Artifacts are retained per retention policy — we recommend 30 days for rolling rollback and longer for compliance.
[24:58] Priya: How long do you keep logs for forensic purposes? Can we extend to 7 years if needed?
[25:05] Maya: Yes, long-term retention is an add-on. Practically we stream to your cold storage and you control retention. Seven years is possible via archive lifecycle policies.
[25:18] [40:00 approximate mark — wrap up segment]
[40:02] Maya: OK I'll recap — action items are: share BCDR runbook and sample RTO/RPO matrix, provide SOC2/ISO reports under NDA, prepare failover topology diagrams and cost deltas, and schedule tabletop. Anything else?
[40:19] Aisha: Please include the explicit SLA credit table and the named escalation list.
[40:24] Maya: Will do. Any questions from the team?
[40:29] Tom: None from me.
[40:30] Priya: No.
[40:31] Evan: Add our legal contact — Connor Hsu — we'll send contact info.
[40:36] Maya: Perfect. We'll get the docs out by Monday. Thanks everyone.
[40:42] [call ends]
